11
Soon we will celebrate the 35th anniversary of 
India’s ground breaking reforms. In 1991, India 
made a quiet but revolutionary admission: the 
state is not a good businessman. Decades of 
license-permit-quota raj had produced scarcity, 
inefficiency, and stagnation. The liberalisation that 
followed did not weaken the state, it redirected 
it. The government stepped back from producing 
goods and stepped forward as a regulator, and 
enforcer of fair rules. The results are well known.
We have yet to apply the same logic to education. 
And the cost of that delay is visible in every 
classroom.
The Convenient Double Standard
Post-liberalisation India has largely settled the 
debate about the private sector’s role in economic 
growth. Even the most committed statists no 
longer argue that the government should occupy 
the commanding heights of the economy. The 
consensus is clear: for the production of economic
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
growth. Even the most committed statists no 
longer argue that the government should occupy 
the commanding heights of the economy. The 
consensus is clear: for the production of economic 
goods, the state’s job is to enable - to facilitate, 
regulate, and enforce contracts - not to produce.
Yet the moment the conversation shifts to 
social goods like education and healthcare, 
this consensus evaporates. Suddenly, state 
production is not only acceptable but necessary. 
The justification is intuitive: inequality in access 
to economic goods may be tolerated, but access 
to education must be equal. Since the market 
produces unequal outcomes, the argument goes, 
the state must produce education itself.
This is a reasonable equity concern. It is not, 
however, a sound efficiency argument. And 
confusing the two has cost India enormously.
The answer is not to abandon the state’s role in 
education - it is to redefine it around three specific
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
however, a sound efficiency argument. And 
confusing the two has cost India enormously.
The answer is not to abandon the state’s role in 
education - it is to redefine it around three specific 
shifts: from controller to regulator, from producer 
to financier, and from inspector to informer.
From Controller to Regulator
There is a meaningful difference between 
a controller and a regulator, and it matters 
enormously in education. A controller decides who 
can enter the market, what they can charge, how 
they must operate, and punishes deviation from 
its own preferences. A regulator sets minimum 
standards, monitors compliance, and protects the 
consumer. One suppresses the system, while the 
other disciplines it.
India’s education system is still governed by the 
controller mindset. Starting a school or college 
remains a bureaucratic obstacle course. Quality 
institutions are scarce. The evidence is visible: high 
tuition fees, large donations, and long admission
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
remains a bureaucratic obstacle course. Quality 
institutions are scarce. The evidence is visible: high 
tuition fees, large donations, and long admission 
queues are not signs of greed, they are signs of 
shortage. Constrained supply meeting aspirational 
demand. The license-permit-quota raj did not 
disappear after 1991, it migrated into education.
What the system needs instead is an independent 
education regulator: an arm’s-length body with a 
clear, bounded mandate. The National Education 
Policy recognises that quality monitoring cannot 
sit inside the same department that runs schools. 
You cannot be both player and referee. The ideal 
is a fully independent regulator, insulated from 
political pressure and departmental interest, and 
that is worth continuing to fight for.
In practice, however, many state governments 
have assigned regulatory functions to their State 
Councils of Educational Research and Training 
(SCERTs). SCERTs are not perfect regulators-

-they are too close to the government, too 
under-resourced, and too often pulled in multiple 
directions. But if they are going to serve this 
function, the question becomes: what can they 
realistically do well?
The answer is assessment. SCERTs should 
focus on systematically assessing the learning 
outcomes of every child in every school - 
government and private. Not to rank students, 
schools, districts, or states. Not to produce 
league tables that shame teachers or trigger 
administrative panic. This data should be kept 
deliberately low-stakes. Their sole purpose 
should be to inform schools and teachers about 
how their students are actually doing, and then to 
trust schools to use that information to improve 
their teaching and learning. Schools that wish to 
publish their data in a format useful to parents 
should be free to do so. But the data should not 
become a weapon, it should remain a mirror.

their teaching and learning. Schools that wish to 
publish their data in a format useful to parents 
should be free to do so. But the data should not 
become a weapon, it should remain a mirror.
From Inspector to Informer
The regulator’s second role is one of information, 
not inspection. The traditional model of school 
inspection-periodic visits, checklists, compliance 
reports-has produced little evidence of improving 
school quality anywhere in India. It consumes 
administrative energy and generates paperwork. 
What parents actually need is not an inspector’s 
report. They need honest, comparable, accessible 
information about how schools are performing.
The regulator, whether an independent body or 
SCERT, should compile and publish information 
on how schools perform in board examinations 
and other competitive assessments for entry into 
colleges. This does not require generating new 
data. The data already exists. What is missing
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
on how schools perform in board examinations 
and other competitive assessments for entry into 
colleges. This does not require generating new 
data. The data already exists. What is missing 
is a neutral, trusted body that aggregates it, 
standardises it, and puts it in the public domain in 
a form that parents can actually use.
Beyond exam results, the regulator should 
create a standard reporting format, building on 
the existing UDISE framework, that all schools, 
government and private, are required to complete 
and publish on their own websites. The regulator 
compiles this data across all schools and makes 
it publicly available in one place, in machine-
readable format. This would allow parents to 
compare schools meaningfully, and enable 
researchers to develop new insights into how 
India’s schools actually function. Transparency 
of this kind costs relatively little and produces 
accountability that no inspection regime has 
managed to deliver.

India’s schools actually function. Transparency

managed to deliver.
The regulator, in this conception, is less an 
enforcer and more an informer - making the 
system legible to the people it is supposed to serve.
From Producer to Financier
The equity concern at the heart of public education 
is real and must be taken seriously. But the 
instrument for addressing it need not be state 
production. There is a crucial difference between 
the state financing education and the state 
producing it. Conflating the two has given India a 
system that is neither equitable nor efficient.
The reform should happen in two steps
The first is decentralisation within the 
government school system itself. Today, 
government school principals operate with far 
less authority than their counterparts in private

13
schools. They cannot make basic decisions about 
how their schools are run, how resources are 
deployed, or how teaching is organised. The 
education department controls everything from a 
distance, with predictably poor results. This must 
change. Government school principals should 
have the same operational authority as private 
school principals. The education department’s 
role should shift to that of a board of trustees or of 
directors, setting broad expectations, evaluating 
outcomes, and holding leadership accountable 
rather than micromanaging daily operations.
The second step is financial autonomy. School 
funding should be converted into a broadly 
defined per-student formula allocation that 
goes directly to the school, giving principals real 
budgetary authority. Teacher salaries, which 
represent the largest cost and the most sensitive 
political variable, can initially continue to be paid
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
budgetary authority. Teacher salaries, which 
represent the largest cost and the most sensitive 
political variable, can initially continue to be paid 
directly by the education department. But non-
salary resources - for materials, maintenance, 
programmes, and school-specific needs - should 
flow to principals to deploy as they see fit. A 
principal with a budget and accountability for 
outcomes is a fundamentally different actor than 
one who must route every request through a 
distant bureaucracy.
For students who cannot afford private schooling, 
the state should act as financier - through 
scholarships, education vouchers, and loans. 
A poor parent armed with a voucher has real 
power: the ability to choose the school that best 
serves their child, rather than accepting whatever 
the state assigns them. That is genuine equity. 
Not the hollow promise of a seat in an under-
resourced, understaffed government school with 
no meaningful accountability to the family it is
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
the state assigns them. That is genuine equity. 
Not the hollow promise of a seat in an under-
resourced, understaffed government school with 
no meaningful accountability to the family it is 
supposed to serve. This new system can initially 
supplement the 25% seats reserved in private 
schools and then slowly subsume it.
This combination of autonomous government 
schools, per-student funding, and demand-side 
support for the poor allows both private and public 
sectors to do well for their students. They both 
respond to demand, innovate, and compete for 
students. The state stops trying to be a controller 
and becomes instead a guarantor of access and a 
monitor of quality.
The Mindset Shift India Needs
India did not become an economic success story 
by having the government produce more. It 
succeeded by redirecting state energy toward 
what the state can actually do well: set standards, 
enforce them fairly, fund those left behind by the
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
by having the government produce more. It 
succeeded by redirecting state energy toward 
what the state can actually do well: set standards, 
enforce them fairly, fund those left behind by the 
market, and get out of the way of enterprise.
Education needs the same clarity of thinking. 
The reforms required are not radical, they are the 
logical extension of what India already believes 
about the economy, applied to the classroom.
From controller to regulator. From producer to 
financier. From inspector to informer.
India’s economy had its 1991 moment. Its 
education system needs it badly and soon.
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

India’s ambition to become a developed nation 
by 2047, Viksit Bharat, will be won or lost in 
its classrooms. This makes a quiet but seismic 
shift in Indian school education, almost entirely 
overlooked in policy circles, impossible to ignore 
any longer.
Over the past two decades, India’s public 
investment in education has grown 
substantially. The combined education spend 
by the Centre and all states rose from ₹94,484 
crore in 2005-06, representing 2.88 % of GDP, 
to ₹8,30,000 crore in 2024-25, or 4.1 % of 
GDP. Government school teachers grew from 
38.6 lakh to 59.1 lakh. Nearly every rupee was 
spent, and every post was filled with sincerity 
of intent. And yet, in 2006, 53.1 % of Class 5 
children in rural India could read a Class 2 text. 
By 2024, that number had fallen to 44.8 %. 
Spending more produces less learning. That is 
the central, uncomfortable fact of Indian school
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

children in rural India could read a Class 2 text. 
By 2024, that number had fallen to 44.8 %. 
Spending more produces less learning. That is 
the central, uncomfortable fact of Indian school 
education today. India’s parents noticed before 
its policymakers did. And they acted.
A System Built by Families, Not the State
In 2005, private unaided schools enrolled 1.57 
crore children, just 10.6 % of the total school 
population. By 2024, that number stood at 9.57 
crore, accounting for 38.8 % of all enrolled 
students. The number of private unaided 
schools grew from 1.42 lakh to 3.39 lakh. 
Teachers in these schools expanded from 3.75 
lakh to an extraordinary 39.6 lakh, a ten-fold 
increase achieved without a single government 
appointment order, without pension liabilities, 
and without public subsidy.
This is not a story of elite schools capturing 
wealthy families. Approximately 82 % of private 
unaided schools in India charge a monthly fee
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

and without public subsidy.
This is not a story of elite schools capturing 
wealthy families. Approximately 82 % of private 
unaided schools in India charge a monthly fee 
of less than ₹2,000. These are neighbourhood 
schools in the community, often a few classrooms 
in a rented building, serving the children of daily-
wage workers, small traders, and first-generation 
aspirants. Families earning ₹10,000-₹20,000 
a month are choosing to spend 7-15% of their 
income on school fees. That sustained, voluntary, 
economic sacrifice across crores of households is 
a democratic verdict, and it is the most important 
data point in Indian education that no government 
report leads with.

that official narratives rarely credit to the right 
source. The proportion of 6-14 year olds in

2024, an achievement celebrated as a triumph

The Problem is not the Schools, but the Rules
And yet, despite their scale and social function, 
private unaided schools operate in a climate of 
regulatory uncertainty that would be unacceptable in 
any other sector with this level of ambition. Across 
28 states and 8 union territories, school operators 
navigate a maze of inconsistent, overlapping, and 
often archaic requirements on land, infrastructure, 
teacher qualifications, compensation, 
recognition, affiliation, and fee revision. A 
school legally operating in Madhya Pradesh may 
face insurmountable barriers in Maharashtra. 
Recognition processes stretch into years. Fee 
revision approvals are discretionary and opaque. 
Inspections are unpredictable. The cumulative effect 
is that the schools most trusted by low-income 
families are also the most legally precarious.
This is not a minor inconvenience. It is a structural
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
is that the schools most trusted by low-income 
families are also the most legally precarious.
This is not a minor inconvenience. It is a structural 
failure. When compliance costs are high and 
arbitrary, it is the small, lean, genuinely affordable 
school that suffers most. The regulatory burden 
falls hardest on those serving the poorest children.
The Case for Ease of Operating Schools
India needs a fundamental reorientation in how 
it approaches private school regulation from 
a posture of suspicion and control to one of 
enablement and accountability. The framework 
must be grounded in principles of transparency, 
predictability, proportionality, accountability, and 
autonomy. Transparent rules, publicly available 
and consistently applied. Predictable timelines 
for recognition and renewal, with no room for 
discretionary delay. Proportionate norms that 
recognise a 150-student neighbourhood school 
and a 2,000-student CBSE campus cannot be 
governed in the same way.
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

discretionary delay. Proportionate norms that 
recognise a 150-student neighbourhood school 
and a 2,000-student CBSE campus cannot be 
governed in the same way.
A concrete mechanism to drive this shift would be 
an Ease of Operating Schools Index - a systematic, 
annual, state-by-state ranking of how simple or 
burdensome it is to establish, run, and sustain 
a private school. India’s Ease of Doing Business 
reforms demonstrated that public rankings create 
a competitive spirit in state governments to act. 
The same logic applies here.

currency of growth. Roads, ports, factories, and 
digital infrastructure are vital, but they will take us 
only halfway. Our children are our greatest asset.

to radical reforms that expand choice for students,

Every society seeks better educational outcomes. Far 
fewer ask a more fundamental question: what kinds 
of institutions make those outcomes possible?
The answer shapes not only its schools, but also 
its economy and politics. India’s educational 
debate is largely concerned with outcomes. We 
measure enrolment, literacy, infrastructure, 
and examination results. We compare states on 
educational performance and evaluate schools by 
what they achieve. Yet a prior question receives 
far less attention. What are the institutional 
conditions that make educational excellence 
possible? Before a child enters a classroom, before 
a teacher begins instruction, and before learning 
outcomes can be measured, an entire architecture 
of laws, regulations, approvals, inspections, and 
administrative procedures determines whether a 
school can exist, operate, innovate, expand, or even
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
of laws, regulations, approvals, inspections, and 
administrative procedures determines whether a 
school can exist, operate, innovate, expand, or even 
survive. Educational outcomes might be visible, but 
educational governance is often invisible.
The Republic Beyond the State
This distinction is not merely administrative. 
It is constitutional. The Constitution of India 
embodies a commitment to both public purpose 
and civic initiative. While the state bears important 
obligations in advancing educational opportunity, 
as reflected in Article 21A, the Indian constitutional 
order has never rested on a monopoly conception 
of educational provision. Instead, it has historically 
accommodated a pluralistic architecture in 
which governments, charitable trusts, religious 
institutions, community organisations, 
philanthropic actors, and educational 
entrepreneurs all contribute to the advancement of 
a common public purpose. Educational pluralism
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
institutions, community organisations, 
philanthropic actors, and educational 
entrepreneurs all contribute to the advancement of 
a common public purpose. Educational pluralism 
is therefore not a deviation from the constitutional 
vision; it is one of its defining features.
India’s educational history confirms this. Many 
of its most enduring institutions emerged not 
from bureaucratic planning but from social 
initiative. Citizens built schools, communities 
sustained them, and philanthropy expanded them. 
Educational progress has often been the result of 
partnership rather than monopoly.
Gandhi’s Swaraj, Tagore’s Freedom
The intellectual foundations of this idea run 
deep. In Hind Swaraj, Mahatma Gandhi argued 
that freedom meant more than political 
independence. Swaraj was ultimately about 
self-governance, the ability of individuals 
and communities to shape the institutions 
that govern their lives. Rabindranath Tagore 
similarly resisted the mechanisation of
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
self-governance, the ability of individuals 
and communities to shape the institutions 
that govern their lives. Rabindranath Tagore 
similarly resisted the mechanisation of 
education. He believed that education should 
cultivate free and creative minds, not merely 
produce administrative conformity.
C. Rajagopalachari (Rajaji), later warned against 
the dangers of the Licence-Permit-Quota Raj. His 
insight extended beyond economics. Societies do 
not become more capable simply because they 
become more regulated. Excessive control often 
weakens the very initiative upon which progress 
depends. B.R. Shenoy made a related argument 
through economics. Knowledge, he observed, is 
dispersed throughout society. No central authority 
possesses sufficient information to direct complex 
human systems effectively.

Friedrich Hayek’s idea of spontaneous order.

Education is a powerful example of this principle. 
No ministry can fully understand the needs of 
every child, every family, every neighbourhood, 
and every school in a country as diverse as 
India. Educational excellence emerges from 
the combined efforts of parents, teachers, 
school leaders, community organisations, 
philanthropists, social entrepreneurs, and 
governments acting within an enabling 
institutional framework.
The Enabling State
The central challenge of educational governance 
is therefore not the production of rules. It is the 
design of institutions. This challenge can be 
understood through a simple framework: of governance. The central lesson was that 
prosperity could not be commanded into existence 
through administrative controls. The role of the

through administrative controls. The role of the

from gatekeeper to institutional architect. Three 
decades later, education confronts a similar 
challenge. The debate is no longer whether non-
state actors should participate in schooling. Indian 
parents have already answered that question. 
Millions of families have exercised agency in 
choosing educational institutions they believe 
serve their children best. The real question is

recognise this reality.

This is the intellectual foundation of the Ease of

of regulation. Nor is it the accumulation of controls.

and upholds standards. But it also recognises 
that educational excellence requires autonomy,

Unfortunately, regulatory systems often drift 
toward a different equilibrium. Freedom is rarely 
extinguished through a single prohibition. More 
often, it is eroded through the cumulative weight 
of approvals, renewals, inspections, certifications, 
and discretionary controls. What begins as 
oversight gradually becomes micromanagement.

educational governance what economic freedom 
indices have done for economic governance. It 
seeks to make visible the quality of the rules that 
shape educational enterprise, civic initiative, 
and institutional innovation by measuring the  
performance of educational governance itself.
Competitive Federalism for Educational 
Excellence
At the same time, the Index advances another 
important constitutional value: competitive 
federalism. Education is a Concurrent List subject, 
and states possess substantial authority over 
school regulation. Yet reform requires comparison. 
What gets measured can be compared. What can 
be compared can be improved. By evaluating 
regulatory frameworks across states, the EoOS

healthy competition, and evidence-based reform.

nation by 2047 will depend on the quality of 
its human capital. But human capital is not 
produced by expenditure alone. It emerges from 
institutions that empower individuals, strengthen 
communities, and enable excellence. For behind 
every learning outcome lies a governance

a set of institutions. And behind every institution

Executive Summary
India’s Next Education Reform Challenge
Much of India’s education debate focuses on what 
happens inside schools. Policymakers discuss 
learning outcomes, teacher quality, curriculum 
reform, infrastructure, financing, and educational 
technology. These are all critical concerns. Yet 
far less attention is paid to the institutional 
environment within which schools operate; the 
rules, regulations, and governance systems that 
shape whether schools can establish themselves, 
function effectively, adapt to changing needs, and 
sustain their educational mission over time.
Before a school can improve learning outcomes, 
recruit teachers, invest in infrastructure, 
or serve students, it must first navigate 
a regulatory framework. Recognition 
requirements, land and infrastructure norms, 
reporting obligations, compliance mandates, 
inspection mechanisms, fee regulations,
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
a regulatory framework. Recognition 
requirements, land and infrastructure norms, 
reporting obligations, compliance mandates, 
inspection mechanisms, fee regulations, 
governance provisions, and administrative 
procedures collectively determine the conditions 
under which schools operate. These regulations 
shape not only how schools are governed, but 
also what they are capable of achieving.
This question assumes particular importance in 
contemporary India. Over the past two decades, 
private unaided schools have emerged as a major 
pillar of the country’s educational ecosystem. 
Today, they educate nearly four out of every ten 
students while constituting less than one-quarter 
of all schools. Their growth has been driven not by 
government mandate, but by the choices of millions 
of families seeking educational opportunities for 
their children. Across metropolitan cities, small 
towns, and rural communities, private schools have 
become an indispensable component of India’s
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
of families seeking educational opportunities for 
their children. Across metropolitan cities, small 
towns, and rural communities, private schools have 
become an indispensable component of India’s 
schooling landscape.
Yet while educational outcomes are routinely 
measured and compared, educational governance 
remains largely invisible. We know far more about 
how students perform than about the regulatory 
environments within which schools function. As 
a result, an important dimension of education 
reform has remained underexplored. The Ease of 
Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 has been 
developed to address this gap.
The EoOS Index is India’s first comprehensive 
comparative assessment of the regulatory 
environment governing private unaided schools 
across states. Rather than measuring educational 
outcomes, the Index measures educational 
governance. It evaluates the extent to which state-
level regulatory frameworks enable schools to
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
across states. Rather than measuring educational 
outcomes, the Index measures educational 
governance. It evaluates the extent to which state-
level regulatory frameworks enable schools to 
establish themselves, operate effectively, mobilise 
resources, undertake institutional transitions, and 
exercise autonomy while remaining accountable 
to public objectives.
Drawing upon a systematic review of state 
education actslaws, rules, regulations, and 
important government orders, notifications, 
circulars, and other legally operative instruments, 
the Index assesses 28 states and 2 union territories 
across six domains of school governance: 
Regulatory Clarity, Regulatory Compliance, 
Protection Against Arbitrary Regulatory 
Action, Financial Sustainability and Resource 
Mobilisation, School Lifecycle Operations, and 
Institutional Autonomy.
To the best of our knowledge, this represents 
one of the first systematic attempts globally to 
evaluate the ease of operating schools through
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
Institutional Autonomy.
To the best of our knowledge, this represents 
one of the first systematic attempts globally to 
evaluate the ease of operating schools through 
a comprehensive legal and regulatory lens. In 
doing so, the Index seeks to bring educational 
governance into mainstream policy discourse and 
provide policymakers with a practical framework 
for regulatory reform.
The purpose of the Index is not to advocate the 
absence of regulation. Schools perform a vital 
public function and must remain accountable to

students, parents, and society. The question is not 
whether schools should be regulated. The question 
is whether regulation enables schools to fulfil their 
educational mission.
What the Index Reveals
The findings of the EoOS Index reveal a striking 
reality: schools in India do not operate within 
a single regulatory environment. They operate 
within distinct state-level regulatory ecosystems 
that vary significantly in their design, quality, and 
degree of enablement.
The variation observed across states is substantial. 
Some states have developed comparatively 
transparent, predictable, and enabling regulatory 
frameworks that support institutional functioning 
while maintaining accountability. Others continue 
to rely on systems characterised by greater 
complexity, administrative discretion, and limited 
institutional flexibility. The resulting differences 
have important implications for how schools are
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
to rely on systems characterised by greater 
complexity, administrative discretion, and limited 
institutional flexibility. The resulting differences 
have important implications for how schools are 
established, governed, financed, and sustained.
At one level, the findings are encouraging. 
Many states have made notable progress in 
codifying regulations, formalising procedures, 
and improving the accessibility of regulatory 
information. The strongest-performing domain 
nationally is Regulatory Clarity, suggesting 
that states have invested considerable effort 
in defining and communicating regulatory 
requirements. Schools today generally operate 
within more structured and visible regulatory 
systems than they did in previous decades. 
Yet the findings also reveal a deeper and more 
consequential reality. India’s school regulatory 
architecture is considerably more developed in 
governing schools than in enabling schools.
The strongest-performing dimensions of the
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
consequential reality. India’s school regulatory 
architecture is considerably more developed in 
governing schools than in enabling schools.
The strongest-performing dimensions of the 
Index relate primarily to defining obligations, 
monitoring compliance, and administering 
oversight. The weakest-performing dimensions 
relate to financial sustainability, institutional 
adaptability, and operational autonomy. Simply 
put, states generally perform better in telling 
schools what they must do than in creating 
conditions that allow schools to succeed. This 
pattern emerges consistently across domains and 
points towards three structural challenges that 
characterise school regulation in India.
The Sustainability Deficit: Schools today are 
expected to satisfy an expanding range of 
obligations relating to infrastructure, staffing, 
safety, compliance, reporting, and educational 
quality. However, the Index finds that regulatory 
frameworks remain considerably less developed

text:
obligations relating to infrastructure, staffing, 
safety, compliance, reporting, and educational 
quality. However, the Index finds that regulatory 
frameworks remain considerably less developed 
in supporting financial sustainability and resource 
mobilisation. Across states, regulatory approaches 
appear substantially more focused on controlling 
institutional behaviour than on enabling long-
term institutional viability. Schools are expected 
to do more, but often with limited flexibility to 
mobilise the resources necessary to meet those 
expectations.
The Adaptability Deficit: Educational institutions 
are dynamic organisations. They expand, 
innovate, introduce new programmes, respond to 
demographic shifts, and evolve to meet changing 
educational needs. Yet the Index reveals that 
regulatory frameworks governing institutional 
transitions remain among the weakest dimensions 
of school governance nationally. States generally 
possess detailed frameworks governing school

text:
regulatory frameworks governing institutional 
transitions remain among the weakest dimensions 
of school governance nationally. States generally 
possess detailed frameworks governing school 
establishment and recognition, but comparatively 
limited mechanisms supporting institutional 
evolution. Schools can enter the system more 
easily than they can adapt within it.
The Trust Deficit: Schools are expected to 
deliver educational outcomes, maintain 
standards, comply with regulations, and 
serve students effectively. Yet many continue 
to operate within frameworks that provide 
relatively limited decision-making authority. 
Institutional autonomy emerges as one of the 
weakest-performing domains in the Index. 
This suggests that schools are frequently 
entrusted with responsibility without being 
granted corresponding authority. The strongest-
performing states demonstrate that accountability

and autonomy can coexist. However, this balance 
remains uneven across much of the country.
Taken together, these findings reveal a regulatory 
architecture that is stronger on control than 
enablement, stronger on compliance than 
capability, and stronger on oversight than 
institutional resilience.
Towards an Enabling Regulatory State
The findings of the EoOS Index do not suggest 
that regulation should be weakened. Rather, 
they suggest that regulation should be improved. 
India’s educational governance challenge is no 
longer one of regulatory absence. It is increasingly 
a question of regulatory design.
Three decades ago, India recognised that 
prosperity could not be achieved through 
administrative control alone. The reforms of 1991 
transformed the relationship between the state and 
the economy by shifting the emphasis from control 
towards enablement. The state did not withdraw
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
transformed the relationship between the state and 
the economy by shifting the emphasis from control 
towards enablement. The state did not withdraw 
from its responsibilities; it redefined them. School 
education today confronts a similar challenge.
The next generation of education reform will 
depend not only on curriculum design, public 
expenditure, technology adoption, or learning 
assessments. It will also depend on the quality 
of the institutional environment within which 
schools operate. The objective is not to choose 
between accountability and autonomy, or 
between regulation and flexibility. The objective 
is to build regulatory systems capable of 
balancing both. The findings of the Index point 
towards five principles that should guide this 
transition.
First, clarity must replace opacity. Schools should 
be able to easily identify, understand, and comply 
with the rules that govern them.
Second, predictability must replace discretion.

transition.
First, clarity must replace opacity. Schools should 
be able to easily identify, understand, and comply 
with the rules that govern them.
Second, predictability must replace discretion. 
Regulatory certainty is essential for institutional 
planning, investment, and long-term 
sustainability.
Third, transparency must accompany 
accountability. Regulatory systems should support 
institutions in meeting educational objectives 
rather than merely monitoring compliance against 
them.
Fourth, governance architecture must integrate 
regulatory neutrality .Governance architecture 
must integrate regulatory neutrality. Similar 
schools should be subject to similar rules, 
regardless of who operates them.
Finally, sustainability should be recognised as 
a legitimate public policy objective. Educational 
quality depends not only on standards and 
oversight, but also on the long-term viability of 
educational institutions.
These principles align closely with the vision

oversight, but also on the long-term viability of

These principles align closely with the vision 
articulated in the National Education Policy 
2020, particularly its emphasis on transparency,

and “light but tight” regulation. The findings of 
the EoOS Index suggest that this transition has 
begun, but remains incomplete.

operate. A regulatory system that combines

strength and prosperity of a nation is, in large 
measure, a reflection of the character, skills, and 
capabilities of its people. If people are provided 
with conditions to develop their capabilities, 
only then can a state fully realise its social and

realise their potential and participate more

the most important institutions through which 
the goal of education is realised.For schools to 
effectively discharge this responsibility, it is 
important that they function under conditions 
which allow them a meaningful existence that

Evolution of School Education Governance 
in India
Since independence, India’s school education 
system has undergone a steady expansion of state 
involvement through constitutional, legislative, 
and policy interventions aimed at widening 
access, improving equity, and standardising 
educational provision. While these reforms 
sought to advance important public objectives, 
they also contributed to the gradual emergence of 
an increasingly complex regulatory environment 
governing schools.
The National Policies on Education of 1968 
and 19862 laid the foundations for a nationally 
coordinated approach to schooling, emphasising 
universalisation, equity, and common standards. 
India’s ratification of the United Nations 
Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC)3  in 
1992 further strengthened the policy commitment 
towards children’s educational entitlements.

Selection of Indicators and Sub-indicators
Indicators and sub-indicators were identified 
through a systematic review of legal and

and operation of private schools. The selection 
process was guided by three criteria:
1.   Regulatory Relevance – The provision must 
directly affect the establishment, operation,

Coding Framework
All indicators are coded such that higher scores 
consistently reflect a more enabling regulatory 
environment and greater ease of operating 
schools. Where provisions reduce administrative 
burden, improve transparency, strengthen 
safeguards, or shorten procedural timelines, they 
receive higher scores. Conversely, provisions that 
increase complexity, uncertainty, or compliance 
burdens receive lower scores.
Normalisation
Since sub-indicators are measured using different 
scales, values are normalised using a min-max 
transformation. This converts all observations 
onto a common scale ranging from 0 to 1, enabling

INSTITUTIONAL AUTONOMY
Introduction
Every regulatory system must answer a 
fundamental question: Who should make 
decisions? Should decisions regarding the 
operation of schools be made primarily 
by regulators, or should they be made by 
educational institutions themselves? This 
question lies at the heart of educational 
governance.
Governments have legitimate responsibilities 
to establish standards, protect student welfare, 
ensure accountability, and safeguard public 
interests. At the same time, schools are complex 
institutions operating within diverse educational, 
social, and economic contexts. They are often 
best positioned to understand their own needs, 
challenges, and opportunities. The challenge for 
policymakers is therefore not whether schools

Introduction
The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 is 
often discussed in the context of curriculum 
reform, foundational learning, multidisciplinary 
education, teacher development, and educational 
quality. Less frequently acknowledged is the 
fact that NEP 2020 is also one of India’s most 
significant governance reform documents.
Beyond its educational objectives, the policy 
articulates a clear vision for the future of 
educational regulation . It recognises that 
educational quality is influenced not only by 
what schools teach, but also by the regulatory 
environment within which they operate. 
Accordingly, NEP 2020 seeks to move educational 
governance towards a framework characterised by 
transparency, institutional autonomy, separation 
of functions, reduced compliance burdens, and 
what it famously describes as “light but tight” 
regulation.

the extent to which this vision is reflected in 
contemporary state-level regulatory frameworks. 
The purpose of this chapter is not to evaluate the 
implementation status of NEP 2020 as a whole. 
Rather, it is to examine how the regulatory

Compliance-Centric Regulatory Model. Within this

by the ability to monitor institutions rather than 
by the ability to enable institutions. This helps

The Sustainability Deficit
The weakest-performing domain in the Index 
is Financial Sustainability and Resource 
Mobilisation. This finding deserves particular 
attention. Financial sustainability is not simply 
another regulatory issue. It is a foundational 
condition for institutional viability. Schools 
cannot recruit teachers, maintain infrastructure, 
invest in technology, or improve educational 
quality without adequate financial resources. Yet 
the findings suggest that regulatory frameworks 
devote relatively limited attention to the question 
of how schools are expected to sustain themselves 
over time. This creates what may be described as a 
Sustainability Deficit. 
Schools are expected to comply with an expanding 
range of obligations while operating within 
frameworks that provide comparatively limited 
support for resource mobilisation and financial
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
Schools are expected to comply with an expanding 
range of obligations while operating within 
frameworks that provide comparatively limited 
support for resource mobilisation and financial 
resilience. The result is a regulatory architecture 
that specifies what institutions must do without 
adequately addressing how those obligations 
are to be financed. This deficit is particularly 
significant because it affects the long-term 
viability of educational institutions themselves.
The Adaptability Deficit
The findings relating to School Lifecycle 
Operations reveal a second structural 
weakness. Educational institutions are dynamic 
organisations. They expand, contract, relocate, 
restructure, innovate, and respond to changing 
educational needs. However, the findings suggest 
that regulatory frameworks often treat schools as 
relatively static entities. States generally possess 
detailed provisions governing establishment and 
recognition. Far fewer possess equally developed

text:
relatively static entities. States generally possess 
detailed provisions governing establishment and 
recognition. Far fewer possess equally developed 
frameworks governing institutional evolution. 
This creates what may be described as an 
Adaptability Deficit.
Schools operate in dynamic environments but 
often encounter regulatory systems designed 
around static assumptions. The result is increased 
friction when institutions seek to adapt, innovate, 
or respond to changing circumstances. In a rapidly 
evolving educational landscape, this deficit may 
become increasingly significant.
The Trust Deficit
The findings relating to Institutional Autonomy 
reveal a third structural challenge. Schools are 
expected to deliver educational outcomes, satisfy 
regulatory requirements, maintain standards, and 
serve students effectively. Yet many continue to 
operate within frameworks that provide relatively 
limited decision-making authority. This creates

serve students effectively. Yet many continue to 
operate within frameworks that provide relatively 
limited decision-making authority. This creates 
what may be described as a Trust Deficit.
Institutions are entrusted with responsibility 
but not always with corresponding authority. 
The result is a governance model in which 
accountability is frequently accompanied by 
extensive operational control. The strongest-
performing states suggest that this trade-off may 
be unnecessary. Accountability and autonomy 
are not mutually exclusive. Indeed, the findings 
indicate that effective governance often depends 
upon balancing the two.

The Governance Identity Problem
The findings also reveal a deeper tension within 
school regulation. Private schools occupy a 
distinctive position within India’s regulatory 
framework. Unlike public institutions, they 
are expected to mobilise their own resources, 
absorb operational risks, and sustain themselves 
financially. Unlike commercial enterprises, 
they operate within frameworks that impose 
significant restrictions on financial discretion 
and institutional autonomy. The result is a 
hybrid institutional model. Schools bear many 
of the responsibilities associated with private 
organisations while operating under constraints 
that limit their ability to function as fully 
autonomous institutions. This creates what may 
be described as a Governance Identity Problem. 
Regulatory systems often expect schools to 
behave like independent institutions without
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
autonomous institutions. This creates what may 
be described as a Governance Identity Problem. 
Regulatory systems often expect schools to 
behave like independent institutions without 
granting them the flexibility typically associated 
with institutional independence. This tension 
appears repeatedly across multiple domains of 
the Index.
The Fee Regulation Paradox
The emergence of fee regulation frameworks 
across many states illustrates this broader 
challenge. In recent years, several states have 
introduced increasingly sophisticated mechanisms 
governing fee determination and fee revisions. 
These interventions are frequently justified on 
grounds of affordability and consumer protection. 
However, the findings reveal an important 
asymmetry. States have increasingly developed 
mechanisms to regulate how schools generate 
revenue, while devoting comparatively less 
attention to how schools sustain themselves. 
The result is what may be described as the Fee 
Regulation Paradox.
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
revenue, while devoting comparatively less 
attention to how schools sustain themselves. 
The result is what may be described as the Fee 
Regulation Paradox.
Regulatory systems often possess more detailed 
frameworks for controlling revenues than for 
supporting sustainability. The challenge is not 
whether fee regulation should exist. The challenge 
is whether financial governance has become 
disproportionately focused on control at the 
expense of viability.
Beyond Regulation versus Deregulation
One of the most important lessons emerging from 
the Index is that educational governance should 
not be framed as a choice between regulation and 
deregulation. The strongest-performing states do 
not necessarily regulate less. Rather, they appear 
to regulate differently. Their frameworks are 
generally characterised by:
• greater clarity;
• stronger predictability;
• reduced procedural fragmentation;
• clearer allocation of responsibilities;
• greater institutional flexibility.

generally characterised by:
• greater clarity;
• stronger predictability;
• reduced procedural fragmentation;
• clearer allocation of responsibilities;
• greater institutional flexibility.
The findings therefore suggest that the future 
challenge for educational governance is not 
reducing regulation but improving regulatory 
design. The question is not how much regulation 
exists. The more important question is whether 
regulation enables institutions to fulfil their 
educational mission.
Towards an Enabling Regulatory State
Taken together, the findings suggest that school 
regulation in India is at an inflection point. The 
past several decades have witnessed significant 
growth in the sophistication of regulatory 
systems governing schools. States have developed 
increasingly detailed frameworks governing 
recognition, compliance, oversight, inspections, 
and accountability. The next stage of reform may 
require a different emphasis.
Rather than focusing exclusively on how schools
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
recognition, compliance, oversight, inspections, 
and accountability. The next stage of reform may 
require a different emphasis.
Rather than focusing exclusively on how schools 
should be regulated, policymakers may need 
to devote greater attention to how schools can 
be enabled. This does not imply abandoning 
accountability. It implies recognising that 
accountability and enablement are complementary 
rather than competing objectives. The strongest 
educational systems are not those that choose 
between regulation and autonomy. They are those 
that successfully balance both.
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

Conclusion
The findings of the Ease of Operating Schools 
Index reveal a regulatory architecture 
characterised by an important structural 
imbalance. Across states, regulatory systems 
appear considerably more developed in 
defining obligations, monitoring compliance, 
and exercising oversight than in supporting 
sustainability, adaptability, and institutional 
autonomy. The result is a governance framework 
marked by three interrelated deficits:
• a Sustainability Deficit;
• an Adaptability Deficit;
• a Trust Deficit.
Taken together, these deficits help explain 
many of the challenges identified throughout 
the Index. The central lesson emerging from the 
findings is therefore straightforward. The future 
challenge for school regulation in India is not 
simply improving compliance or strengthening 
oversight. It is building a regulatory architecture 
that combines accountability with enablement,
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
challenge for school regulation in India is not 
simply improving compliance or strengthening 
oversight. It is building a regulatory architecture 
that combines accountability with enablement, 
oversight with flexibility, and public interest with 
institutional sustainability. Ultimately, schools 
can only deliver educational outcomes if they are 
not merely regulated, but also empowered  
to succeed.
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

of operating schools while preserving accountability and quality assurance mechanisms.

regulatory clarity, transparent access to legal information, and safeguards against arbitrary

while preserving accountability. The state can streamline recognition and operational approvals by 
rationalising NOC requirements, security deposits, and infrastructure-related compliance, adopting 
greater risk-based and digital compliance mechanisms. Simplifying approval processes for school 
establishment, recognition, and institutional changes through single-window, time-bound systems 
would further improve ease of operation. Haryana can also strengthen institutional autonomy by 
providing schools with greater flexibility in governance and academic management, consistent with
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

quality standards. Finally, periodic reviews of fee regulation and compliance requirements can help

for responsible private school participation while maintaining public accountability.

regulatory delivery mechanisms, and institutionalising independent regulatory oversight through an 
autonomous State School Standards Authority. Such reforms would complement the state’s existing 
strengths and help create a more balanced ecosystem that promotes accountability, innovation, and 
educational growth. By improving financial enablement and regulatory modernisation, Punjab is well

on strengthening safeguards against arbitrary regulatory action and improving financial enablement 
while institutionalising regulatory excellence through an independent State School Standards Authority.

a national model for modern, transparent, and innovation-oriented school governance. By combining

Policy Pathway
Uttar Pradesh occupies a unique position within India’s school education landscape, serving the largest 
school-going population in the country and educating more than half of its students through private 
schools. The state’s regulatory framework demonstrates notable strength in financial Mobilisation, 
providing schools with greater scope for financial sustainability and resource planning than is available 
in most jurisdictions. However, these advantages are substantially diluted by high compliance burdens, 
limited institutional autonomy, and challenges in navigating regulatory processes. As one of India’s largest 
and most influential education ecosystems, even incremental improvements in regulatory efficiency could 
have transformative effects on millions of students and thousands of schools. Future reforms should
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
have transformative effects on millions of students and thousands of schools. Future reforms should 
focus on simplifying compliance requirements, improving regulatory accessibility, and empowering 
schools with greater operational autonomy while preserving accountability safeguards. Such changes 
would significantly enhance the ease of operating schools and strengthen the long-term sustainability of 
educational provision across the state.

Centre for Civil Society  |  The Ease of Operating Schools Index 2026
194
Policy Pathway
Uttarakhand presents a regulatory environment with several foundational strengths but significant 
structural gaps. The state performs above the national average in institutional autonomy and regulatory 
compliance, suggesting that schools generally operate within a reasonably consistent compliance 
framework and retain some operational flexibility. It also performs relatively well in school lifecycle 
operations, reducing barriers to institutional continuity. However, these advantages are undermined by 
the complete absence of enabling provisions for financial Mobilisation and comparatively weak protections 
against discretionary regulatory action. Given that private schools educate nearly six out of every ten 
students in the state, strengthening the long-term sustainability of the sector is critical for maintaining
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
students in the state, strengthening the long-term sustainability of the sector is critical for maintaining 
educational access and choice. Future reforms should focus on enabling financial viability, improving 
regulatory transparency, and strengthening procedural safeguards while preserving the state’s existing 
strengths in compliance management and institutional flexibility. Such measures would create a more 
balanced and enabling regulatory environment for schools across Uttarakhand.

Centre for Civil Society  |  The Ease of Operating Schools Index 2026
198
Policy Pathway
West Bengal can improve its Ease of Operating Schools by strengthening regulatory certainty while 
preserving accountability. The state should simplify and consolidate school regulations through a 
single, publicly accessible regulatory portal that provides comprehensive guidelines, standard operating 
procedures, timelines, and application tracking. Procedural safeguards should be strengthened by 
limiting discretionary inspections, introducing risk-based inspection mechanisms, removing inspection 
costs borne by schools, and establishing transparent appeal and grievance redress systems. Financial 
regulations should be made more enabling by streamlining fee revision approvals, providing greater 
flexibility in fund utilisation, and ensuring timely RTE reimbursements. School lifecycle processes, 
including recognition and upgradation, should be digitised with time-bound approvals. Building on its
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
including recognition and upgradation, should be digitised with time-bound approvals. Building on its 
relatively stronger institutional autonomy, West Bengal can align its regulatory framework with the 
principles of transparency, predictability, proportionality, and ease of compliance envisioned under NEP 
2020’s “light but tight” regulatory approach.

Definitions of Indicators 
DOMAIN 1 - Regulatory Clarity, Predictability & Accessibility (2 Indicators, 41 sub-indicators)
Indicator 1: Regulatory Transparency - This indicator assesses the accessibility of regulatory information 
relevant to school. It examines the availability of laws, manuals, circulars, guidance documents, and digital 
support systems through official State Education Department websites and portals. 
Indicator 2: Procedural Predictability - This indicator evaluates if schools are able to anticipate 
administrative decision-making with certainty. Accordingly, it maps clarity of timelines, approving 
authorities, and codification of administrative procedures. 
DOMAIN 2 - Regulatory Compliance ( 7 Indicators, 27 sub-indicators)
Indicator 1: Compliances during school establishment - This indicator covers procedural and financial
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
DOMAIN 2 - Regulatory Compliance ( 7 Indicators, 27 sub-indicators)
Indicator 1: Compliances during school establishment - This indicator covers procedural and financial 
requirements for obtaining permission to establish schools. It includes certifications, fees, deposits and 
other compliance-related conditions during the stage of opening schools. 
Indicator 2: Infrastructure norms for school recognition - This indicator broadly covers all infrastructure 
related requirements mandated by the laws for getting the schools recognized by the state governments.  
It includes compliances like facilities provided, classroom sizes, and nature of land, etc. 
Indicator 3: Procedure for Fee Hike - This indicator covers different steps and documentary requirements 
imposed on schools for seeking approval for fee hikes. 
Indicator 4: Staffing requirements - This indicator assesses the staffing requirements, particularly the prescribed
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
imposed on schools for seeking approval for fee hikes. 
Indicator 4: Staffing requirements - This indicator assesses the staffing requirements, particularly the prescribed 
teacher-student ratios. It examines the extent to which staffing standards are fixed through the legal norms. 
Indicator 5: Financial Reporting - This indicator evaluates accounting and financial disclosure-related 
obligations imposed on schools. It also assesses the frequency of such reporting and the consequences for 
non-compliance with these requirements. 
Indicator 6: Affiliation related requirements - This indicator covers certifications relevant for obtaining 
affiliation from state boards of education. 
Indicator 7: Capital requirements for recognition- This indicator measures the financial prerequisites 
imposed on schools as part of the recognition process. The sub-indicators assess capital adequacy and 
deposit related requirements during this stage.
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
imposed on schools as part of the recognition process. The sub-indicators assess capital adequacy and 
deposit related requirements during this stage. 
DOMAIN 3 - Operations without Arbitrary Regulatory Action (4 indicators, 52 sub-indicators)
Indicator 1: Inspections- This indicator evaluates school inspection procedures on the basis of their 
safeguards and objectivity. In doing so, it highlights the scope of discretionary risk, along with the 
availability of procedural protections and appellate mechanisms for schools.
Indicator 2: Withdrawal of Affiliation - This indicator analyses procedural protections available in cases 
where the state boards withdraw their affiliation granted to schools. 
Indicator 3: Withdrawal of approvals and takeover powers - This indicator evaluates the procedural 
protections available during the withdrawal of approvals such as permission to establish and school
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
protections available during the withdrawal of approvals such as permission to establish and school 
recognition, as well as during the takeover of school management or property. It also examines the 
availability of appellate mechanisms for schools in such cases.
Indicator 4: Parent Grievance Redressal - This indicator evaluates the procedural safeguards available to 
schools in fee-related complaints raised by parents. It examines the availability of hearing opportunities, 
penalties, and appellate mechanisms in such proceedings.

DOMAIN 4 - Financial Mobilisation (3 indicators, 18 sub-indicators)
Indicator 1:  Fee Collection and Utilization of Funds - This indicator assesses regulatory controls over fee 
structures. It also examines limitations on the use of school revenues and savings by schools. 
Indicator 2: Mechanism for fee approvals - This indicator covers processes and approvals involved for fee 
fixation and its revision. It determines the extent of regulatory oversight in fee-related decision-making 
and procedural safeguards available in these approval processes.
Indicator 3: Regulations on capitation fee - This indicator assesses the extent to which the legal framework 
restricts or permits the charging of capitation fees by schools. It examines prohibitions, exceptions, and 
penalties relating to the charging of capitation fees under the applicable legal framework.
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
penalties relating to the charging of capitation fees under the applicable legal framework. 
DOMAIN 5: School Lifecycle Operations ( 5 Indicators, 16 sub-indicators)
Indicator 1: School Establishment Requirements - This indicator covers steps involved for obtaining a 
permission to establish schools and the scope of power available with authorities to withdraw such 
permission.
Indicator 2: School Operation and Expansion Requirements - This indicator broadly covers permissions 
required for school operations and upgradation, which includes approvals and state government 
recognition.
Indicator 3: Board Affiliation - The indicator covers procedures for obtaining and retaining board affiliation. 
This includes norms for inspections, and consequences arising from violation of affiliation norms.
Indicator 4: Voluntary Exit - This indicator assesses if permissions are required if the school wishes to 
voluntarily close itself, and punishments for violating such norms.
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
Indicator 4: Voluntary Exit - This indicator assesses if permissions are required if the school wishes to 
voluntarily close itself, and punishments for violating such norms. 
Indicator 5: Forced Exit - This indicator assesses the conditions under which the government has powers to 
close down a school or take over its property. 
DOMAIN 6: Institutional Autonomy (2 Indicators, 10 sub-indicators)
Indicator 1: Payment of Staff Salaries - This indicator analyses the extent schools have power to fix staff 
salaries. 
Indicator 2: Self Governance - This indicator covers the regulatory requirements governing constitution, 
composition, functioning, and reconstitution of School Management Committees (SMCs). It also examines 
if the authorities have power to take actions against the SMC.

Dr Animesh Kumar
Dr Animesh Kumar is a Senior Legal Researcher at CCS. As an advocate, he has argued various matters 
related to civil and criminal disputes at various judicial forums across India. His doctoral research 
investigated Women’s political participation in the PRIs in the State of Bihar. He has published various 
articles on education. His specialisation includes constitutional law, with a research focus on women’s 
political participation. At the Centre for Civil Society, he has authored the Nagaland State Regulatory 
Profile which maps the laws governing K-12 education system in the State and reviewed multiple working 
papers dealing with school education.
Animesh is the recipient of the Best Paper Presentation Award 2024 at ICRE 2.0 at Nirma University, 
Gujarat (India). He has served as Co-Chair for numerous technical sessions at national and international
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

text:
Gujarat (India). He has served as Co-Chair for numerous technical sessions at national and international 
seminars and conferences. He has also edited three scholarly volumes titled Decentralization in India, 
Alternative Dispute Resolution in India, and Law & Social Change. Additionally, Animesh is associated 
with various international & national journals as an editor and advisory editorial board member. He is the 
Editor-in-Chief of a peer-reviewed journal, Lex Revolution, ISSN 2394-997X (Print),  3107-282X (Online).
Shaivy Maheshwari
Shaivy Maheshwari is an Advocate enrolled with the Bar Council of Delhi. She has pursued her LLM in 
International Trade and Business Laws from NALSAR, Hyderabad and BALLB(H) from Symbiosis Law 
School, Noida. At the Centre for Civil Society, Shaivy has authored Bihar State Regulatory Profile, which 
maps laws, institutions, and education governance in Bihar; and co-authored a working paper on “For-

maps laws, institutions, and education governance in Bihar; and co-authored a working paper on “For-
profit Schooling in India Law, Limits, and Loopholes.” Having previously worked at CCS, Shaivy brings 
experience in the areas of public governance, education, and livelihood. Alongside trade and competition 
law, she brings legal expertise particularly in the domain of Constitutional Law and Administrative Law. 
Prior to joining CCS, she has interned with various think tanks and research organizations such as NITI

Nitesh Anand
Nitesh Anand is Associate Director, Policy Research & Training at the Centre for Civil Society (CCS) and 
Advisor to the Department of Policy, Ministry of Education, Youth and Sport, Cambodia. A Friedrich-
Naumann-Stiftung Scholar, India Fellow, and graduate of the Technical University of Munich, Nitesh
source: The Ease of Operating Schools (EoOS) Index 2026 - Centre for Civil Society

Advisor to the Department of Policy, Ministry of Education, Youth and Sport, Cambodia. A Friedrich-
Naumann-Stiftung Scholar, India Fellow, and graduate of the Technical University of Munich, Nitesh 
works on education, governance, and regulatory reform across Asia, leading research, policy engagement, 
and capacity-building initiatives with governments, think tanks, academic institutions, and civil society 
organizations.
Current work explores liberalising educational governance, institutional innovation, regulatory 
modernization, legal design, and participatory governance. Guided by a commitment to individual freedom 
and effective public institutions, this work seeks to create enabling environments that expand opportunity, 
strengthen accountability, and foster human flourishing.

Disclaimer
All measures have been undertaken to guarantee the precision, thoroughness, and impartiality of the Ease 
of Operating Schools Index 2026. The findings are derived from a comprehensive analysis of applicable 
legal and regulatory frameworks which are publicly accessible as of December 2025. The assessment 
primarily adopts a de jure perspective, encapsulating the authors’ interpretation and evaluation of the 
legal and regulatory provisions applicable during the study period.
Considering the intricate nature of regulatory frameworks and the potential for varied interpretations of 
legal provisions, it is plausible that readers may reach conclusions that diverge from those articulated in 
this report. The scores, rankings, and observations should be regarded as indicative and are intended to 
promote informed discourse regarding regulatory governance of school education.
